admitted_primitives_probed.detail: C-immutable items -- but the CONTAINER is rebindable
C-immutable value -- but any holder is rebindable

strongest_candidate_design_tested: Anchor sealed state to the identity of the resolver's live _by_ref / _by_key containers AND re-derive a relation fingerprint from live _by_ref at decision time. This was implemented and tested.

strongest_candidate_result.conclusion: The commission's required invariant is NOT establishable inside the current pure-Python owner boundary.
strongest_candidate_result.coordinated_attack_description: replace victim._by_ref and victim._by_key with substituted containers and rebind the ledger cell to a state re-anchored to those containers in one step; the victim then returns TEMPORAL_DIRECTIONAL_CLAIM_AUTHORIZED using the source's genuine relation and custody material

what_would_be_required: custody material held outside the Python object graph, or
an unforgeable native/extension-level capability object, or
process isolation with an IPC boundary, or
an immutable, kernel/OS-backed handle (e.g. a sealed file descriptor or keychain-backed token) that the owner holds opaquely
why_no_pure_python_anchor_survives: Only C-level VALUES resist (tuple items, int attributes). But custody is a mapping from owner to material, so custody must live in some CONTAINER. Every Python-level container the owner can reach is also reachable by the admitted caller, and every one of them is re-assignable: closure cell (cell_contents), module global, class attribute, instance attribute (even on frozen dataclasses and __slots__), function defaults, function __code__, property, or WeakKeyDictionary (whose keys are attacker-controlled through __eq__/__hash__). Therefore any secret the owner holds is READABLE by the caller, and any value derived from it (including semantic_hash, which is public) is RECOMPUTABLE. Consequently no custody binding built from Python-visible state can be non-forgeable.
